mainTopic: Whether an אומן holding someone's item can claim it, the role of עדים in giving and returning a deposit, and how רבה reads the related ברייתות.
overview: This amud continues a discussion of an אומן (craftsman) who is holding someone's item. First the גמרא asks whether a deposit given in front of עדים can be returned without them. It answers that it must be returned in front of עדים, so the craftsman cannot claim 'I gave it back.' Then אביי brings a ברייתא about a slave held by a craftsman and a cloak held by a launderer. The גמרא first clarifies the ברייתא. In its second case, רבה explains that a third person is believed because of a מיגו: he could have said 'I bought it from you.' אביי then challenges רבה from the word 'he saw' in the first case. רבה answers that there were עדים and the owner also had to see the item. When אביי points out that this clashes with רבה's own rule about returning before עדים, רבה says he retracted it. Finally רבא brings a ברייתא about a dispute over a craftsman's fee to support רבה. He begins to show that it must be a case without עדים, and his proof continues on the next amud.

steps.title: Does a deposit made before witnesses not need witnesses to be returned?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא tests an idea that seems to follow from the discussion: maybe a deposit given in front of witnesses can be returned without witnesses.
steps.simpleTranslation: Someone who deposits an item with his friend in front of witnesses: does that mean the friend does not need to return it to him in front of witnesses?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא raises a question to test a possible idea. It is setting up the next step, where it will reject that idea.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The question is whether giving an item over in front of witnesses also requires witnesses when it is given back. If no witnesses were needed for returning it, the holder could just say 'I already gave it back.' The question is said with surprise, as if this would be a strange rule.

keyTerms.meaning: One who deposits an item with someone for safekeeping
With his fellow, meaning another person
In front of witnesses
To return

phrases.english: One who deposits an item with his fellow in front of witnesses,
does he not need to have it returned to him in front of witnesses?

steps.triggerLanguage: הַמַּפְקִיד אֵצֶל חֲבֵירוֹ בְּעֵדִים אֵינוֹ צָרִיךְ לְהַחְזִיר לוֹ בְּעֵדִים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the earlier discussion of the אומן from before this section, testing an idea that seems to follow from it.
steps.kashyaTarget: The earlier ruling that an אומן who received the item in front of עדים cannot claim the item as his own.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If a deposit given in front of עדים could be returned without עדים, the craftsman could have said 'I already returned it to you' and been believed. Because of that מיגו, he should also be believed when he says 'I bought it.'

steps.title: Rejected: a deposit given before witnesses must be returned before witnesses
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rejects the idea: something deposited in front of witnesses must also be returned in front of witnesses.
steps.simpleTranslation: Do not think that. Rather, someone who deposits with his friend in front of witnesses must have it returned to him in front of witnesses.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא says the idea from Step 1 is wrong. It states the correct rule: witnesses at the start mean witnesses are needed at the return.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Because the item was handed over in front of witnesses, the holder cannot simply claim 'I gave it back' without witnesses to back him up. This closes off that claim for the אומן in the earlier case.

keyTerms.meaning: Do not think that; that idea is wrong
Rather
Needs to; must

steps.whatToRemember: A deposit that was handed over in front of witnesses must be returned in front of witnesses. Without them, the holder cannot claim he gave it back.

phrases.english: Do not think so!
Rather, one who deposits an item with his fellow in front of witnesses
must have it returned to him in front of witnesses.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the idea raised in Step 1.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Rejects the idea and states the correct rule
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Maybe witnesses are needed only when the item is first handed over, not when it is returned.
steps.terutzMaskana: Witnesses are needed for the return too, so the holder cannot claim he returned it.

steps.title: אביי brings the ברייתא of the slave and the cloak
steps.stepSummary: אביי quotes a ברייתא: a craftsman who claims the owner sold him the item or gave it to him is not believed, but a claim of 'you told him in my presence to sell it' is accepted.
steps.simpleTranslation: אביי objected from a ברייתא: A man saw his slave in the hands of a craftsman, or his cloak in the hands of a launderer. He said to him, 'What is it doing with you?' If the holder says 'You sold it to me' or 'You gave it to me as a gift,' his words mean nothing. If he says 'In my presence you told him to sell it or give it to him as a gift,' his words stand.
steps.whatsHappening: אביי brings a ברייתא to challenge רבה. The ברייתא has two cases: in the first the holder is not believed, and in the second his words stand.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the first case the craftsman is not believed, because his holding the item does not prove he owns it. In the second case, a claim that the owner told someone to sell or give the item is accepted. אביי first clarifies the second case (steps 4-5), and then builds his actual challenge from the word 'he saw' in the first case (step 6).

keyTerms.meaning: An objection is raised from a teaching of the תנאים
A craftsman
A launderer
What is it doing with you?
He has said nothing; his claim is not accepted
His words stand; his claim is accepted

steps.confusionAlert: Do not get lost in the second case: 'him' (the one told to sell) and 'him' (the one receiving the item) can be different people. The next steps explain exactly who is speaking.

phrases.english: אביי raised an objection:
If one saw his slave in the hands of a craftsman,
or his cloak in the hands of a launderer,
and he said to him: 'What is it doing with you?'
If he answers: 'You sold it to me,'
or 'You gave it to me as a gift,'
he has said nothing.
But if he says: 'In my presence you told him to sell it'
'or to give it to him as a gift,'
his words stand.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a challenge to רבה's ruling, using a ברייתא.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבה's position that whether the item was handed over in front of עדים decides if the אומן can claim it
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The first case of the ברייתא says the owner 'saw' his item with the craftsman. אביי will argue (step 6) that this must be a case without עדים, and still the owner wins. That clashes with רבה's view that עדים are the deciding factor.

steps.title: What is the difference between the two cases of the ברייתא?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why the holder is not believed in the first case but is believed in the second.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is different about the first case, and what is different about the second case?
steps.whatsHappening: Before going on, the גמרא stops to understand the ברייתא. It asks why the two cases end differently.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Both claims sound similar: the owner gave up the item. Yet 'You sold it to me' is not accepted, while 'You told him to sell it' is. The גמרא wants to know what makes the second claim stronger.

keyTerms.meaning: What is different?
The first part of a teaching
The last part of a teaching

phrases.english: What is different about the first case,
and what is different about the second case?

steps.triggerLanguage: מַאי שְׁנָא רֵישָׁא וּמַאי שְׁנָא סֵיפָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks a clarifying question about the ברייתא quoted in Step 3.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Why the holder's claim is rejected in the first case but accepted in the second.

steps.title: רבה: the second case is about a third person, believed through a מיגו
steps.stepSummary: רבה explains that the second case is about a different person who got the item, and he is believed because he could have just said 'I bought it from you.'
steps.simpleTranslation: רבה said: The second case is where the item comes out of the hands of another person. That other person says to the owner: 'In my presence you told him to sell it or give it as a gift.' Since he could have said 'I bought it from you,' when he says 'In my presence you told him to sell it,' his words stand and he is believed.
steps.whatsHappening: רבה answers the question. The second case is not about the craftsman at all, but about another person who now holds the item.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Unlike the craftsman, this other person could have simply claimed 'I bought it from you' and been believed. So when he makes a weaker claim, that the owner told the craftsman to sell or give it, he is also believed. This reasoning is called a מיגו: since he could have made a stronger claim, his weaker claim is accepted.

keyTerms.meaning: Where the item comes out of the hands of another person
Since; he is believed because he could have made a better claim
If he wanted
I bought it
He is believed

steps.whatToRemember: The craftsman himself is not believed. In the second case of the ברייתא, the one believed is a third person, and he is believed because of a מיגו: he could have said 'I bought it from you.'
steps.whyThisMatters: This answer keeps the rule that a craftsman's holding the item proves nothing. It shows that the case where a claim is accepted is really about someone else.

phrases.english: רבה said:
The second case is where the item comes out of the hands of another person,
phrases.notes: The 'other person' is not the craftsman. He is someone who now has the item.

phrases.english: and that other person says to the owner:
'In my presence you told him to sell it'
'or to give it as a gift.'
Since, if he wanted, he could have said to him:
'I bought it from you,'
so when he says to him instead:
'In my presence you told him to sell it,'
his words stand, and he is believed.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבָּה סֵיפָא בְּיוֹצֵא מִתַּחַת יְדֵי אַחֵר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of Step 4 by explaining who the speaker in the second case is.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The second case is about a third person, not the craftsman. He is believed through a מיגו, because he could have claimed he bought the item from the owner.

steps.title: אביי's challenge from the words 'he saw'
steps.stepSummary: אביי says the opening case of the ברייתא must be one with no עדים. If so, seeing the item alone lets the owner take it back, which goes against רבה.
steps.simpleTranslation: The first part of the ברייתא says 'he saw.' What case is this? If there are עדים, why do we need 'he saw'? Just bring the עדים and take the item! So it must be a case with no עדים, and still, once the owner saw it, he may take it.
steps.whatsHappening: אביי now uses the ברייתא to attack רבה. He argues that the owner wins just by seeing his item, even without עדים.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבה had made עדים the key factor. אביי argues that the word 'he saw' would be pointless if עדים were present, so the case must have no עדים. Even so, the craftsman is not believed, which seems to show that seeing the item is enough without עדים.

keyTerms.meaning: The first part of a teaching
What are the circumstances? What case is this?
Let him bring witnesses and take it
Seizes, takes hold of

phrases.english: In any event, the first clause teaches: "he saw."
phrases.notes: This is the ברייתא from step 3, where the owner saw his item in the craftsman's hands.

phrases.english: What are the circumstances?
If there are witnesses,
why do I need "he saw"?
Let him bring witnesses and take it!
Rather, is it not where there are no witnesses?
And when he saw it, he may seize it in any case!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the ברייתא was explained in step 5, אביי returns to its opening clause to challenge רבה.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבה's position that the deciding factor is whether the item was given before עדים
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If there were עדים, the word 'he saw' would add nothing. So the case has no עדים, and the owner still wins because he saw the item.

steps.title: רבה: there are witnesses, and he also saw it
steps.stepSummary: רבה answers that the ברייתא is about a case with עדים. The owner wins only if he also sees the item in the craftsman's hands now.
steps.simpleTranslation: No. Really there are עדים, and the rule applies only where he saw it.
steps.whatsHappening: רבה defends himself. The case does have עדים, and 'he saw' is a second condition that is also needed.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The עדים show that the item was handed over, and 'seeing' shows it is still with the craftsman. Without the seeing, the craftsman could claim he bought it, because he has a מיגו: he could have said 'I gave it back.'

keyTerms.meaning: Actually, really (keeping the original reading)
And that is only where...

phrases.english: No, actually it is where there are witnesses;
and that is only where he saw it.
phrases.notes: Seeing it with the craftsman right now takes away his chance to say "I already gave it back."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers אביי's challenge by redefining the case of the ברייתא.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Redefining the case: both עדים and seeing are needed
steps.terutzHavaAmina: 'He saw' means there were no עדים.
steps.terutzMaskana: There were עדים, and seeing is an extra requirement that blocks the claim 'I returned it.'

steps.title: אביי: that clashes with your own rule
steps.stepSummary: אביי reminds רבה that he himself ruled that a deposit given before עדים must be returned before עדים. Under that rule, the craftsman could never claim he returned it.
steps.simpleTranslation: But you are the one who said: someone who deposits with his friend before עדים must have it returned before עדים!
steps.whatsHappening: אביי attacks רבה's answer using רבה's own earlier rule.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבה's answer depends on the craftsman being able to say 'I returned it' without עדים. But according to רבה's rule from step 2, a deposit given before עדים can only be returned before עדים. Then the craftsman has no such claim, so seeing the item should not be needed.

keyTerms.meaning: But you are the one who said
One who deposits an item
To pay it back, to return it

phrases.english: But you are the one who said:
One who deposits with his friend in front of witnesses
must return it to him in front of witnesses!
phrases.notes: This is the rule from step 2.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the answer in step 7 as contradicting רבה's own rule.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבה's answer that seeing is needed even when there are עדים
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If a deposit given before עדים must be returned before עדים, the craftsman cannot claim he returned it, so the extra condition of 'seeing' is pointless.

steps.title: רבה: I took that rule back
steps.stepSummary: רבה admits that he changed his mind about returning a deposit before עדים.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: I have retracted.
steps.whatsHappening: רבה answers by saying he no longer holds the rule אביי quoted.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Now רבה holds that a deposit given before עדים can be returned without עדים. So the craftsman could say 'I returned it,' and that is why the owner must see the item to win.

keyTerms.meaning: I have retracted, I changed my mind

steps.whatToRemember: רבה's final view: a deposit given before עדים does not need to be returned before עדים. In the ברייתא, the owner needs both עדים and seeing the item.

phrases.english: He said to him: I retracted.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Resolves אביי's contradiction by withdrawing the earlier rule.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: A deposit given before עדים must be returned before עדים.
steps.terutzMaskana: It may be returned without עדים, so the craftsman would have a claim of 'I returned it.'

steps.title: רבא brings a ברייתא about a craftsman's fee to support רבה
steps.stepSummary: רבא quotes a ברייתא about a dispute over a craftsman's pay. Who must bring proof depends on whether the cloak is still with the craftsman and how much time has passed.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא brought a ברייתא to support רבה. Someone gives his cloak to a craftsman. The craftsman says, 'You agreed to pay me two,' and the owner says, 'Only one.' As long as the cloak is with the craftsman, the owner must bring proof. If the craftsman already gave it back: on time, he swears and takes his pay. If the time passed, whoever wants to take money from the other must bring proof.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא quotes a ברייתא to back up רבה. Here the גמרא is setting up the source; the support drawn from it comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא shows that holding the cloak gives the craftsman a strong position, so the owner must prove his side. Once the cloak is returned, the craftsman loses that advantage. He is believed with an oath only on time, and afterward he must bring proof.

keyTerms.meaning: Raises a question from a source (usually a challenge)
To support
You fixed, you set (a price)
He swears and takes
The one who wants to take from another must bring proof

steps.confusionAlert: The word מֵתִיב usually brings a challenge. Here it is used to support רבה, not to attack him.

phrases.english: Rava raised an objection to support Rabba:
One who gives his cloak to a craftsman,
the craftsman says: You set two for me,
phrases.notes: Two coins as his fee for the work.

phrases.aramaic: וְהַלָּה אוֹמֵר: לֹא קָצַצְתִּי לְךָ אֶלָּא אַחַת.
phrases.english: and the other says: I set only one for you.
As long as the cloak is in the craftsman's hand,
the owner must bring proof.
If he gave it to him: within its time,
phrases.notes: "Its time" means the day the cloak was returned.

phrases.english: he swears and takes.
If its time passed,
the one who takes from his friend bears the burden of proof.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After רבה's position is settled, רבא brings outside support for it.
steps.raayaObject: רבה's position on a craftsman holding an item and what he is believed to claim
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא about a dispute over a craftsman's fee while the cloak is in his hands or after it was returned

steps.title: What case is the ברייתא about? It cannot be one with witnesses
steps.stepSummary: רבא asks what situation the ברייתא describes. He rules out a case with עדים, because then the עדים could tell us what pay was agreed.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is the case? If there are witnesses, let us just see what the witnesses say!
steps.whatsHappening: רבא is asking what kind of case the ברייתא from step 10 is describing. He tests one option, a case with עדים, and shows it does not work. This sets up the next move.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the ברייתא, someone has to bring proof about the craftsman's pay. If עדים had watched the cloak being handed over, they would have heard the agreed price, so nobody would need to rely on who is believed. Since the ברייתא does not just send us to the עדים, it must be a case without עדים.

keyTerms.meaning: What does the case look like? (a question asking for the exact situation)
If there are witnesses
Let us see / let us look at
What are they saying?

steps.confusionAlert: רבא is not concluding anything yet. He knocks out the option with עדים so that the ברייתא will turn out to be a case without עדים. That is what he will use as his proof.

phrases.english: What are the circumstances?
phrases.notes: רבא is asking about the ברייתא he just quoted, the one about the craftsman's pay.

phrases.english: If it is where there are witnesses,
let us see what the witnesses say!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: רבא starts analyzing the ברייתא he brought in step 10 to find out exactly which case it describes.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What is the exact case of the ברייתא? Were there עדים to the handing over of the cloak or not?
steps.kashyaTarget: The possibility that the ברייתא is talking about a case with עדים.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: With עדים, the dispute over the pay would be settled by their testimony, so the ברייתא's rules about who must bring proof would not be needed.
